plan.angle: Lane A (log 'lane: A' in metadata), series 'Life on GLP-1'. Hook (15 s or less): a one-line news hook (The Conversation, Oct 22, 2026, on GLP-1 nausea needing closer study), then the first answer: 'In the big trials, the most common side effects were stomach-related (nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, vomiting). Most were mild to moderate and happened mostly while the dose was being stepped up.' Use only the paper's wording for that timing. Chapters named as searched questions: (1) What are the most common tirzepatide side effects? Give SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM 2022; adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes; 72 weeks) rates for each dose arm vs placebo, with group sizes, copied exactly. Add one SURPASS line, labelled as type 2 diabetes. (2) Why does tirzepatide cause nausea? Slower stomach emptying and appetite signalling, citing the Neurogastroenterol Motil review and the label. (3) When do side effects get better? Only what the trials and label report, presented as averages, not predictions. (4) What helps with nausea and constipation? Habits recommended by the 2025 joint nutrition advisory and expert consensus: smaller meals, eating slowly, stopping when comfortably full, fewer greasy meals, fluids (unless you've been told to limit fluids), and adding fibre gradually. Say 'recommended', never 'proven on tirzepatide'. (5) What else can happen? Injection-site reactions, plus discontinuation-for-side-effects rates vs placebo from the paper. (6) When to call your prescriber? Take the warning signs from the label exactly: severe or persistent belly pain (pancreatitis), gallbladder symptoms, dehydration with vomiting or diarrhoea, low blood sugar when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas, and the boxed thyroid warning in label wording. No dosing or titration talk, and never 'adjust your dose'. Re-hook every 45–75 s. The subscribe ask comes after the 'what helps' payoff. 'Don't stop, switch or change your medicines on your own.' End by naming 'How Long Does Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Take to Work?' as the video to watch next, then the full prescriber line. 8–12 min, 14:00 ET. Thumbnail (4 words or fewer): a relieved, labelled tummy character next to a tirzepatide pen, with text like 'Easier First Weeks'.

Tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) side effects: which are common and what helps.

Quick answer: In SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM, 2022; adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes), nausea, diarrhea, constipation and vomiting were most common, mostly mild to moderate and mainly during dose escalation. More than 9 in 10 people in every tirzepatide group did not stop because of side effects.

This is general information, not personal advice. Don't stop, switch or change your medicines on your own. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether tirzepatide is right for you.

scenes.section: Tirzepatide side effects in 15 seconds
scenes.narration: If you've felt that mix of hope and worry, you're not alone, and it makes total sense. Let's answer her questions one at a time.

scenes.section: What are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.narration: Question one: what are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.retention_device: Chapter named after the searched question

scenes.section: What are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.narration: The clearest data come from a trial called SURMOUNT-1, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in twenty twenty-two.

scenes.section: What are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.narration: It followed two thousand five hundred thirty-nine adults with obesity, or with overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes, for seventy-two weeks.

scenes.section: What are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.narration: They were randomly assigned to weekly tirzepatide at five, ten or fifteen milligrams, or to placebo: six hundred thirty, six hundred thirty-six, six hundred thirty and six hundred forty-three people.

scenes.section: What are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.narration: Nausea topped the list. It was reported by twenty-four point six percent on five milligrams, thirty-three point three percent on ten, and thirty-one percent on fifteen, versus nine point five percent on placebo.

scenes.section: What are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.narration: So on the two higher doses, roughly one in three people felt nauseous at some point. Flip that around: about two in three didn't.

visual.stat_label: had nausea on tirzepatide 10 or 15 mg

scenes.retention_device: Humanised number with a reassuring flip

scenes.section: What are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.narration: Diarrhoea came next: eighteen point seven, twenty-one point two and twenty-three percent across the three doses, versus seven point three percent on placebo.

scenes.section: What are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.narration: Constipation: sixteen point eight, seventeen point one and eleven point seven percent, versus five point eight on placebo. Notice the twist: it was less common on the highest dose than on the middle one.

scenes.section: What are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.narration: Vomiting was less common: eight point three, ten point seven and twelve point two percent, versus one point seven percent on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Completes the set before a twist

scenes.section: What are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.narration: But here's the number that surprises almost everyone. Look back at the placebo group.

scenes.section: What are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.narration: Nearly one in ten people getting no active drug reported nausea too. Stomachs get upset anyway, which is exactly why trials compare against placebo. The fair comparison is the gap, not the raw number.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the mini-loop plus a way to read the data

scenes.section: What are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.narration: If you have type 2 diabetes, there's a trial closer to you. In SURPASS-2, adults with type 2 diabetes took tirzepatide or semaglutide one milligram for forty weeks, with about four hundred seventy people in each group.
scenes.retention_device: Speaks to a second audience segment

scenes.section: What are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.narration: Nausea was reported by seventeen to twenty-two percent on tirzepatide and eighteen percent on semaglutide. Diarrhoea, thirteen to sixteen versus twelve. Vomiting, six to ten versus eight. Again, mostly mild to moderate. Different people, same pattern: the stomach first.

scenes.section: What are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.narration: The Zepbound label's list of common reactions also includes belly pain, indigestion, injection-site reactions, tiredness, allergic-type reactions, burping, hair loss and acid reflux.

scenes.section: What are the most common tirzepatide side effects?
scenes.narration: But why would a medicine that works through hormones upset your stomach at all? The answer turns out to be the same reason it works.
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: cliffhanger before a section change

scenes.section: Why does tirzepatide cause nausea?
scenes.narration: Question two: why does tirzepatide cause nausea?

scenes.section: Why does tirzepatide cause nausea?
scenes.narration: Tirzepatide activates the receptors for two gut hormones, GLP-1 and GIP. These hormones play a part in appetite and blood sugar.
scenes.retention_device: Simple mechanism, explained like a friend would

scenes.section: Why does tirzepatide cause nausea?
scenes.narration: One effect is written right into the label: tirzepatide delays gastric emptying. Food leaves your stomach more slowly than usual.

scenes.section: Why does tirzepatide cause nausea?
scenes.narration: Picture a sink with the drain partly closed. Pour slowly and it's fine. Tip a big jug in at once and it backs up. That full, queasy feeling is the backup.

scenes.section: Why does tirzepatide cause nausea?
scenes.narration: These hormone signals also act on areas of the brain involved in appetite, so many people feel full sooner and eat less.

scenes.section: Why does tirzepatide cause nausea?
scenes.narration: So the same effect that quiets constant food noise can also make a big, fast meal feel like far too much.
scenes.retention_device: Pays off 'the same reason it works'

scenes.section: Why does tirzepatide cause nausea?
scenes.narration: Dana feels it on day two: half a sandwich, and suddenly she's done. If you've had that 'where did my appetite go?' moment, you're not imagining it.

scenes.section: Why does tirzepatide cause nausea?
scenes.narration: Which brings us to the question Dana really wants answered: does it get better?

scenes.section: When do tirzepatide side effects get better?
scenes.narration: Question three: when do tirzepatide side effects get better?
scenes.retention_device: Chapter named after the searched question

scenes.section: When do tirzepatide side effects get better?
scenes.narration: Here's what the trial actually reports, nothing more. In SURMOUNT-1, stomach side effects occurred primarily during dose escalation, the stretch when doses were being stepped up, which lasted up to twenty weeks.
scenes.retention_device: Direct answer to the open question

scenes.section: When do tirzepatide side effects get better?
scenes.narration: And most of those side effects were mild to moderate in severity.

scenes.section: When do tirzepatide side effects get better?
scenes.narration: The Mounjaro label adds one mechanical clue: the delay in stomach emptying is largest after the first dose, and that effect diminishes over time. That's about stomach emptying, not a promise about how you'll feel.
scenes.retention_device: Surprising detail with an honest caveat

scenes.section: When do tirzepatide side effects get better?
scenes.narration: Remember, these are averages across thousands of people, not a forecast for you. Some people notice very little. Others notice it most around a dose change.

scenes.section: When do tirzepatide side effects get better?
scenes.narration: That's why the pace is a conversation with your prescriber, not something to work out alone. If side effects are rough, tell them, and don't change anything on your own.

scenes.section: When do tirzepatide side effects get better?
scenes.narration: But Dana doesn't have to just grit her teeth. There are practical habits experts recommend, and the third one is the one most people skip.
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: new open loop (the skipped habit)

scenes.section: What helps with nausea and constipation?
scenes.narration: Two sources here: a twenty twenty-five joint advisory from four lifestyle medicine, nutrition and obesity organisations, and an expert consensus on managing the stomach side effects of GLP-1 medicines.

scenes.section: What helps with nausea and constipation?
scenes.narration: One honest caveat: these are recommended habits, based on expert advice. They weren't each tested in a tirzepatide trial.

scenes.section: What helps with nausea and constipation?
scenes.narration: For nausea, the big four are smaller meals, eating slowly, stopping when you're comfortably full, and fewer greasy meals.

scenes.section: What helps with nausea and constipation?
scenes.narration: First: smaller meals. If food leaves your stomach more slowly, a smaller portion simply fits better. Think side plate, not dinner plate.

scenes.section: What helps with nausea and constipation?
scenes.narration: Second: eat slowly. Put your fork down between bites and give your fullness signals time to catch up.

scenes.section: What helps with nausea and constipation?
scenes.narration: Third, the one people skip: stop when you're comfortably full, not when the plate is empty. On these medicines, the gap between satisfied and too much can feel smaller than you're used to.

scenes.section: What helps with nausea and constipation?
scenes.narration: Fourth: go easy on greasy, fried and very rich meals. The experts recommend limiting high-fat foods while your stomach adjusts.

scenes.section: What helps with nausea and constipation?
scenes.narration: That's nausea. Constipation needs a slightly different playbook.

scenes.section: What helps with nausea and constipation?
scenes.narration: Fifth: fluids. Sip water across the day, unless your clinician has told you to limit fluids.

scenes.section: What helps with nausea and constipation?
scenes.narration: Sixth: add fibre gradually. Vegetables, beans, lentils, oats, whole grains. Build up step by step rather than all at once.

scenes.section: What helps with nausea and constipation?
scenes.narration: The advisory also stresses getting enough protein, to help protect muscle while you lose weight. Small, protein-forward meals tick two boxes at once.

scenes.section: What helps with nausea and constipation?
scenes.narration: And if nausea, vomiting or constipation keeps going, tell your prescriber. They can look at what's happening for you, and asking isn't complaining.

scenes.section: What helps with nausea and constipation?
scenes.narration: Imagine Dana a week later. Side plates, slower lunches, a water bottle on her desk. Her stomach isn't perfect, but she feels like she's steering again.

scenes.section: What helps with nausea and constipation?
scenes.narration: If this helped, this is exactly what our 'Life on GLP-1' series is for: practical, evidence-checked answers for everyday life on these medicines. Subscribe, and the next one will find you.

scenes.section: What else can happen on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Injection-site reactions, like redness or itching where you inject. The label reports them more often with tirzepatide than with placebo.

scenes.section: What else can happen on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Now, the number I promised. In SURMOUNT-1, how many people stopped the medicine because of side effects?
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: payoff of the loop opened in the last chapter

scenes.section: What else can happen on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Four point three percent on five milligrams, seven point one percent on ten, and six point two percent on fifteen, versus two point six percent on placebo.

scenes.section: What else can happen on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Put the other way: in every tirzepatide group, more than nine in ten people did not stop because of side effects.

visual.stat_label: didn't stop for side effects, SURMOUNT-1

scenes.retention_device: Humanised number with a hopeful flip

scenes.section: What else can happen on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: One more label point that's easy to miss. Zepbound may make birth control pills work less well for four weeks after starting and for four weeks after each dose increase. If you use the pill, ask your prescriber about other options.

scenes.section: What else can happen on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: And if you're scheduled for surgery or a procedure, tell everyone treating you that you take tirzepatide.

scenes.section: What else can happen on tirzepatide?

scenes.narration: Question six: when should you call your prescriber?
scenes.retention_device: Chapter named after the searched question

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: These aren't the common side effects, but the label is clear that they need prompt attention. Here they are, close to the label's own words.

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: Severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting. You may feel the pain from your belly through to your back. The label lists this as a possible sign of pancreatitis.

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: That's the one I promised. For this sign, the label says to stop using the medicine and call your healthcare provider right away. It's not a wait-and-see sign.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: Gallbladder problems: pain in your upper stomach, fever, yellowing of your skin or eyes, or clay-coloured stools.

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: Vomiting or diarrhoea that leaves you dehydrated. The label warns this fluid loss may make kidney problems worse, and it advises drinking fluids to lower that chance.
scenes.retention_device: Links back to the hydration tip

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: Low blood sugar. If you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea, your risk may be higher. Signs include shakiness, sweating, dizziness, confusion, hunger and a fast heartbeat.
scenes.retention_device: Speaks to the type 2 diabetes viewer

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: A serious allergic reaction: swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, problems breathing or swallowing, severe rash or itching, fainting, or a very rapid heartbeat. The label says to stop using it and get medical help right away.

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: The Zepbound label also asks you to watch for depression or thoughts of suicide. Call your healthcare provider right away if you have changes in mood, behaviour, thoughts or feelings that are new, worse, or worry you.

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: And the boxed warning, the label's most prominent kind. In rats, tirzepatide caused thyroid C-cell tumours. It's unknown whether it causes these tumours, including medullary thyroid carcinoma, in humans.

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: So the label says not to use it if you or a family member have had medullary thyroid carcinoma, or if you have Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type two.
scenes.on_screen_text: MTC or MEN 2: not for you
scenes.retention_device: Who it isn't for, plainly stated

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: Tell your prescriber about a lump or swelling in your neck, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or shortness of breath.

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: Apart from those urgent label instructions, don't stop, switch or change your medicines on your own. Call, describe what's happening, and decide together.

scenes.section: Your tirzepatide side-effect checklist
scenes.narration: Expect the stomach first: nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, vomiting. In the trials, most were mild to moderate and happened mainly during dose escalation.

scenes.section: Your tirzepatide side-effect checklist
scenes.narration: Try the recommended habits: smaller, slower meals, stop when comfortably full, fewer greasy meals, steady fluids, and fibre added gradually.

scenes.section: Your tirzepatide side-effect checklist
scenes.narration: And know your call list: severe belly pain that won't go away, gallbladder signs, dehydration, low blood sugar, allergic reactions, mood changes and neck symptoms.

scenes.section: Your tirzepatide side-effect checklist
scenes.narration: Picture Dana a month in. She knows what's common, what helps, and what's worth a call. She's not scared. She's prepared. That's the goal for you too.

factcheck.summary:
The script is accurate and safe. It passes with three minor wording fixes. Lane A, Life on GLP-1 series.

**What I checked**
- **SURMOUNT-1 figures, all match the paper:** 2,539 adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes, followed 72 weeks. Group sizes 630, 636, 630 and 643. Rates on 5, 10 and 15 mg versus placebo:
  - nausea 24.6, 33.3 and 31.0% versus 9.5%
  - diarrhoea 18.7, 21.2 and 23.0% versus 7.3%
  - constipation 16.8, 17.1 and 11.7% versus 5.8%
  - vomiting 8.3, 10.7 and 12.2% versus 1.7%
  - stopped because of side effects 4.3, 7.1 and 6.2% versus 2.6%
- **SURMOUNT-1 wording:** the quote "mild to moderate in severity, occurring primarily during dose escalation" is the paper's own, and the up-to-20-week dose-escalation period matches the trial design.
- **SURPASS-2:** about 470 per group over 40 weeks, compared with semaglutide 1 mg. Nausea 17–22% versus 18%, diarrhoea 13–16% versus 12%, vomiting 6–10% versus 8%, mainly mild to moderate. All correct.
- **Zepbound and Mounjaro labels:** these match the labels' wording:
  - the list of common reactions
  - delayed stomach emptying, "largest after the first dose and diminishes over time"
  - birth control pills working less well for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase
  - telling your care team before surgery
  - the pancreatitis, gallbladder, dehydration and kidney, low blood sugar (insulin or sulfonylurea) and allergy warnings
  - the boxed warning about rat thyroid C-cell tumours, and not using it with medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2
  - the neck symptoms

**Framing and safety are good:** the placebo comparison is explained, the habits are labelled as expert advice rather than trial-tested, Dana is clearly labelled hypothetical, the fluids tip carries a caveat, there's no dosing advice, the "don't stop, switch or change on your own" line is there, and it ends on the disclaimer plus the prescriber line.

**Sources**
- Both journal papers and the 2025 joint nutrition advisory (AJCN, PMID 40450457) exist.

audio.soundNotes: Music is already well-placed (-13.5 dB under voice, -13.3 in pauses); trimmed it ~0.7 dB overall (gain 0.92) so pauses settle at the -14 dB ceiling while staying inside the -12/-15 band under speech. Fixed a dozen SFX that measured well above the -14/-20 dB speech target (several blips/pops/swooshes hitting -3.5 to -11 dB, including a near-clipping blip at 123.4s and a pop at 591.2s) by cutting their gain roughly 6-12 dB; left the many pause-transition whooshes/swells at -6 to -12 dB alone since that's exactly the reveal/transition target. Added five bespoke SFX (stomach gurgle, draining sink, a single tense heartbeat on the pancreatitis warning, a soft electrical tingle on the allergy cue, and a warm resolving chime on the closing "Not scared, Prepared" beat) to give the serious-symptom section and the emotional button more texture than the stock kit alone provides, all kept modest in level so the narrator stays king.

issues: Green circle 'P' icon is a bit abstract/brand-logo-like rather than an obvious body part, may be slightly ambiguous at a glance, but pairs clearly with the sad stomach for a before/after read
Visual metaphor is confusing: a smiling paper airplane for 'small meal' doesn't read instantly, undermining the stomach-contrast concept
Icons (fries vs plane) don't clearly relate to tirzepatide side effects, risking viewer confusion about what the video is actually about
Heart icon is a strong visual for cardiovascular topics, but this video is about GI/stomach side effects, so the icon mismatches the content and could feel slightly misleading
Headline is generic enough that it could belong to almost any health video, weaker specific curiosity than #0

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are clean and legible at phone size with no cut-off text or clutter. #1's food-vs-plane comparison is the weakest: the plane-as-'small meal' visual pun doesn't land instantly and muddies the connection to the video's actual topic (tirzepatide side effects), which also risks looking like engagement bait. #2 is the cleanest and most curiosity-driven ('Normal or not?'), but the heart icon is a mismatch for a stomach/GI side-effects video and could mislead viewers about the content, and the headline is generic. #0 pairs a clear emotional before/after (sad, queasy stomach turning into a calm, smiling brand icon) with a headline that directly promises relief within the first weeks — exactly what 'side effects and what helps' pays off. It has the clearest single focal story, strong contrast, and no mismatched metaphor, making it the safest highest-CTR choice that stays honest to the title.
